info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 3.2: Deterministic Computer-Assisted Imaging: IIIF, Image Processing, and File Storage.

name.text: 01 Question: The IIIF Vision: Solving the Image Silo Problem

questiontext.text: What problem was IIIF created to solve?

generalfeedback.text: IIIF replaces one-library-one-viewer silos with shared rules, so images from different institutions can be used in the same tool.

answer.text: Digitized images were locked to each library's own website and viewer, so material from different institutions could not be used together.

feedback.text: Correct. That lock-in is what the lesson calls an image silo, and shared rules are what break it.

answer.text: Libraries had not yet digitized enough manuscripts to make comparison worthwhile.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The images existed; the problem was that each institution published them in an incompatible way.

answer.text: Digital images degraded over time and needed a format that would not fade.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital files do not fade; the problem was access and compatibility, not decay.

answer.text: Copyright law prevented scholars from viewing manuscripts held in other countries.

feedback.text: Incorrect. IIIF is a technical standard and does not change the rights in an image.

name.text: 02 Question: The IIIF Image API: The Canonical Request URI Syntax

questiontext.text: In a IIIF image address, what does the part of the path immediately after the identifier specify?

generalfeedback.text: A IIIF image address is a readable recipe: region, size, rotation, quality, format — so you can crop and resize a page by editing a URL.

answer.text: The region: which rectangle of the source image to return, either `full` or pixel coordinates.

feedback.text: Correct. The order is region, then size, then rotation, then quality and format.

answer.text: The size in pixels of the image that will be returned.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Size comes after region; the two are separate parts of the path.

answer.text: The compression quality, from 1 to 100.

feedback.text: Incorrect. `quality` in IIIF means colour treatment (default, gray, bitonal), and it comes later in the path.

answer.text: The identifier of the manifest the image belongs to.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manifests belong to the Presentation API; the Image API path describes pixels only.

name.text: 03 Question: Deep Zoom and Image Tiling

questiontext.text: Why can a browser display a 12,000-pixel-wide manuscript image almost instantly?

generalfeedback.text: Deep zoom works by sending only the small tiles currently on screen, which is why a gigantic manuscript image opens instantly.

answer.text: The server has pre-cut the image into small tiles at several sizes, and the viewer downloads only the tiles currently on screen.

feedback.text: Correct. You are never downloading the whole image, only the few small squares you can actually see.

answer.text: The image is compressed so heavily that the full file is only a few hundred kilobytes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The master stays large; tiling avoids sending it rather than shrinking it.

answer.text: The browser downloads the entire image in the background while showing a placeholder.

feedback.text: Incorrect. With tiling there is no need to transfer the whole file at all.

answer.text: Modern connections are fast enough to transfer several hundred megabytes before the page renders.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That transfer would be slow and wasteful, which is precisely why tiling exists.

name.text: 04 Question: The Image Information Document (`info.json`)

questiontext.text: Why does `info.json` matter when you are writing TEI `` coordinates?

generalfeedback.text: Fetch `info.json` to learn an image's true dimensions, and record which version your coordinates actually describe.

answer.text: It reports the true dimensions of the institution's master, which may be far larger than the copy you downloaded and measured.

feedback.text: Correct. Coordinates describe one specific image, so you must know which version yours describe.

answer.text: It contains the rights statement that determines whether you may crop the image.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Licence information may appear elsewhere; info.json is technical description.

answer.text: It lists the zones the institution has already defined on the page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. info.json describes the image service, not the content of the page.

answer.text: It converts your pixel coordinates into TEI corner attributes automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That conversion is something you or a script must do.

name.text: 05 Question: The IIIF Presentation API: The Shared Canvas Model

questiontext.text: What is a IIIF Canvas?

generalfeedback.text: A IIIF Canvas represents the physical surface, not a file, so several images and a transcription can all be anchored to the same page.

answer.text: An abstract rectangle standing for one physical surface, to which images and transcriptions are attached.

feedback.text: Correct. Because the Canvas is not a file, several images of the same page can be anchored to it.

answer.text: The highest-resolution image file an institution holds for a page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is the master image; a Canvas is not a file at all.

answer.text: The viewer window in which a manuscript is displayed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The Canvas is part of the data model, not part of the interface.

answer.text: A drawing surface on which scholars sketch annotations by hand.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Annotations are data attached to a Canvas, not freehand drawing.

name.text: 06 Question: Anatomy of a IIIF Manifest: Structure and JSON-LD

questiontext.text: Someone sends you 'a IIIF link' for a document. What are you most likely being given, and what should you do with it?

generalfeedback.text: A Manifest is the package a viewer reads, and being able to open one and see what an institution published (and omitted) is a research skill.

answer.text: A Manifest URL, which you can open to see the object's metadata, how many Canvases it has, and what the institution chose to publish.

feedback.text: Correct. Reading a manifest critically — including noticing what is missing — is a research skill.

answer.text: A single JPEG of the first page, which you should download and crop.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A manifest describes the whole object rather than delivering one image.

answer.text: A login page for the institution's reading room booking system.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manifests are public data files, not access controls.

answer.text: A TEI file you can validate against `msdesc.rng`.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manifests are JSON; TEI is XML, and the two use different schemas.

name.text: 07 Question: Multi-Page Structures: Sequences, Ranges, and Structures

questiontext.text: What do IIIF Ranges let a manifest express that a plain list of Canvases cannot?

generalfeedback.text: Ranges group Canvases into a table of contents or into physical gatherings, letting a manifest record both how a book reads and how it was made.

answer.text: Named groupings of Canvases, such as a table of contents or the quires a volume was built from.

feedback.text: Correct. Ranges can record both how a book reads and how it was physically assembled.

answer.text: The pixel dimensions of each page image.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Dimensions belong to the Canvas and the image service.

answer.text: The licence attached to each individual image.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Rights information is separate from structural grouping.

answer.text: The order in which pages were digitized.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ranges describe intellectual and physical structure, not capture history.

name.text: 08 Question: Interoperable Juxtaposition: Comparing Witnesses in Mirador

questiontext.text: What does Mirador make possible, and what is its precondition?

generalfeedback.text: Mirador puts witnesses from different institutions side by side with synchronized zoom, but only when each institution publishes IIIF.

answer.text: Side-by-side comparison of witnesses from different institutions with synchronized zoom, provided each institution publishes IIIF.

feedback.text: Correct. Where an institution does not publish IIIF, that absence is itself a finding about your document.

answer.text: Automatic collation of two texts, producing a list of variants without human reading.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Mirador displays images; collation is a separate process covered in Module 7.

answer.text: Downloading complete high-resolution images from any library for offline use.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Mirador streams tiles and does not override an institution's access terms.

answer.text: Editing and correcting the images held by an institution.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Viewers do not alter the institution's files.

name.text: 09 Question: The Open-Source Imperative in Scholarly Imaging

questiontext.text: Why does this course treat open-source imaging tools as a scholarly requirement rather than a budget preference?

generalfeedback.text: Scholarly imaging uses open-source tools because a claim about an image is only verifiable if someone else can rerun the exact operation.

answer.text: A claim about an image is only verifiable if another scholar can rerun the exact operation and get the same pixels.

feedback.text: Correct. A secret algorithm cannot be checked, and an unverifiable image is weak evidence.

answer.text: Open-source tools produce higher-quality images than commercial ones.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The argument is about verifiability and durability, not image quality.

answer.text: Commercial software is not permitted in university work.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is permitted; the objection is to undocumented, unrepeatable processing.

answer.text: Open-source tools are the only software that can read TIFF files.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Many programs read TIFF; the issue is transparency of the operations.

name.text: 10 Question: Interactive Editing with GIMP: Manual Adjustments and Layer Inspection

questiontext.text: What role does GIMP play in the workflow this lesson recommends?

generalfeedback.text: GIMP is for exploring an image and finding the right settings; the settings you find then go into a script that can be rerun and audited.

answer.text: It is where you explore an image and find the right settings, which then go into a script that can be rerun and audited.

feedback.text: Correct. Explore interactively, then record the decision as a command.

answer.text: It is the final production tool, because hand-adjusting each page gives the best results.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hand-adjusting many pages introduces drift and leaves no record.

answer.text: It converts images into TEI facsimile markup automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. GIMP is an image editor; the markup is written or scripted separately.

answer.text: It is used only for cropping, since its other tools are not accurate enough.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Its curve and channel tools are exactly what make it useful for inspection.

name.text: 11 Question: Scripting with ImageMagick: Command-Line Batch Automation

questiontext.text: Besides speed, what is the scholarly advantage of processing images with an ImageMagick command?

generalfeedback.text: An ImageMagick command applies identical treatment to every page and doubles as the written record of what was done.

answer.text: The command itself is the record of what was done, so anyone can reproduce the result exactly.

feedback.text: Correct. A written command is documentation and instruction at the same time.

answer.text: Commands produce higher-resolution output than graphical editors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Resolution comes from the capture, not from the interface used to process it.

answer.text: Commands avoid any loss of quality, whatever operations are chained.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lossy saves and repeated rotation still cost quality, whatever tool is used.

answer.text: Command-line tools are the only software that can deskew an image.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Many tools deskew; the advantage here is the auditable record.

name.text: 12 Question: High-Performance Processing with libvips: Memory Efficiency and Tiling

questiontext.text: What problem does libvips solve that ImageMagick typically does not?

generalfeedback.text: libvips streams large images in strips, so gigapixel files can be processed and tiled on ordinary hardware.

answer.text: It streams very large images in narrow strips, so gigapixel files can be processed without exhausting memory.

feedback.text: Correct. It is also the standard tool for generating deep-zoom tile pyramids.

answer.text: It corrects colour more accurately than other tools.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Colour correction depends on profiles and targets, not on this tool.

answer.text: It can read formats that ImageMagick cannot open at all.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The difference is memory handling and speed, not format support.

answer.text: It recovers detail from low-resolution images.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No deterministic tool adds detail that was never captured.

name.text: 13 Question: Reproducible Processing: Logging Parameters and Scripting Pipelines

questiontext.text: Which pair of habits makes image processing reproducible?

generalfeedback.text: Keep originals unedited and commit the commands you ran, so every published image can be traced back to the file it came from.

answer.text: Never edit the original in place, and commit the commands you ran alongside your edition.

feedback.text: Correct. This is the same discipline as your Git history, applied to pixels.

answer.text: Save every intermediate version as a JPEG, and note the date of each.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Repeated JPEG saves lose data, and dates do not record what was done.

answer.text: Use the same software version as your institution, and avoid scripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scripts are what make the process repeatable; avoiding them defeats the purpose.

answer.text: Work only in a graphical editor so the changes can be seen as they are made.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Watching a change happen does not record the parameters that produced it.

name.text: 14 Question: Coordinate-Based Cropping: Isolating Folios and Zones

questiontext.text: A crop is specified as `-crop 5100x7000+450+600`. What do those four numbers mean?

generalfeedback.text: Cropping is specified as x, y, width, height — convert carefully, because TEI's `ulx/uly/lrx/lry` are corners instead.

answer.text: A rectangle 5100 wide and 7000 tall, starting 450 pixels from the left edge and 600 from the top.

feedback.text: Correct. Tools use width, height, and offsets, whereas TEI uses two corners — converting between them is where errors happen.

answer.text: The corners of the rectangle, at (5100, 7000) and (450, 600).

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is TEI's convention, not ImageMagick's.

answer.text: A rectangle 450 wide and 600 tall, positioned at 5100, 7000.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The size comes first and the offsets follow the plus signs.

answer.text: A resize to 5100x7000 followed by a 450-pixel border of 600 pixels' opacity.

feedback.text: Incorrect. `-crop` cuts a region; it does not resize or add borders.

name.text: 15 Question: Deskewing and Geometric Alignment: Rectifying Rotational Drift

questiontext.text: Why should a page be deskewed once, from the original, rather than repeatedly?

generalfeedback.text: Deskewing straightens a tilted page so lines and zones align, but rotate once from the original, because each rotation costs sharpness.

answer.text: Each rotation recalculates every pixel from its neighbours, so repeated rotation gradually softens fine strokes.

feedback.text: Correct. One high-quality rotation from the master is harmless; several accumulate damage.

answer.text: Each rotation permanently changes the file's dimensions in a way that cannot be undone.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Dimensions can change, but the real cost is loss of sharpness.

answer.text: Deskewing only works correctly the first time it is applied to a file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It will run repeatedly; the problem is what repeated resampling costs.

answer.text: Repeated deskewing corrupts the file's embedded metadata.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Metadata loss is a separate concern from resampling.

name.text: 16 Question: Contrast Adjustment and Dynamic Range Optimization

questiontext.text: What is the danger of pushing contrast adjustment too far on a faded document?

generalfeedback.text: Contrast stretching separates faded ink from darkened paper, but over-adjusting deletes the faintest evidence entirely.

answer.text: Clipping: the faintest strokes are crushed to solid black and features like watermarks are blown out to white, destroying evidence.

feedback.text: Correct. Over-adjustment does not enhance the evidence; it deletes it.

answer.text: The file size grows to the point where it cannot be served on the web.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Contrast adjustment does not meaningfully change file size.

answer.text: The image's colour profile is discarded, so colours can no longer be corrected.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Profiles are handled separately from tonal adjustment.

answer.text: The coordinates of previously defined zones shift.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tonal changes do not move pixels; cropping and rotation do.

name.text: 17 Question: White Balance and Color Calibration: Applying ICC Profiles and Neutral Ramps

questiontext.text: Why is an uncalibrated colour cast a scholarly problem rather than a cosmetic one?

generalfeedback.text: Photograph a grey or colour reference with the page, so later viewers can tell ageing from lighting.

answer.text: A reader cannot tell whether the paper yellowed with age or the lamp was warm, so a claim about the object's colour becomes unverifiable.

feedback.text: Correct. This is why a grey or colour reference belongs in the frame at capture time.

answer.text: Yellow images are harder to compress and produce larger files.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Colour cast has no meaningful effect on compression.

answer.text: Colour casts prevent text recognition software from running at all.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Recognition may be affected by contrast, but the issue here is evidential.

answer.text: Moodle rejects images that are not in the sRGB colour space.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is about scholarly accuracy, not platform requirements.

name.text: 18 Question: Spatial Filtering: Sharpening and Unsharp Masking

questiontext.text: What does over-sharpening do to a manuscript image?

generalfeedback.text: Modest sharpening clarifies letterforms; heavy sharpening thickens strokes and misrepresents the hand.

answer.text: It leaves bright halos along strokes and thickens letterforms, misrepresenting the hand.

feedback.text: Correct. For palaeography that is a distortion of the evidence, not just an ugly image.

answer.text: It reveals detail that the lens did not capture.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Sharpening boosts edge contrast; it cannot add missing detail.

answer.text: It removes noise from the paper background.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Sharpening usually amplifies noise rather than removing it.

answer.text: It converts the image to greyscale as a side effect.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Sharpening does not change the colour mode.

name.text: 19 Question: Noise Reduction and Defect Masking

questiontext.text: What rule governs how strong a noise filter may be on a historical document?

generalfeedback.text: Use the gentlest possible noise filter, because anything that removes dust can also remove the faintest real marks.

answer.text: The filter must never be larger than the smallest mark that carries meaning, such as a point of punctuation or an accent.

feedback.text: Correct. Anything strong enough to erase dust is strong enough to erase the faintest real marks.

answer.text: Noise filters should be applied at maximum strength, then the image resharpened.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That sequence destroys fine detail and then fakes its edges back.

answer.text: Noise reduction is safe at any strength because it only affects the background.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Filters cannot tell background speckle from faint ink.

answer.text: Noise filters should be applied only to the archival master, never to derivatives.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The master must stay unedited; filtering belongs to derivatives.

name.text: 20 Question: Thresholding and Binarization: From Grayscale to Pure Black and White

questiontext.text: Why does a single whole-page threshold fail on most historical documents?

generalfeedback.text: Local thresholding handles stains and shadows that a single whole-page cut-off ruins, but always keep the greyscale original.

answer.text: Uneven staining and shading mean one cut-off turns a shadowed corner solid black while erasing faint text elsewhere.

feedback.text: Correct. Calculating a threshold locally, for each small area, handles this properly.

answer.text: Historical inks are brown rather than black, so thresholds cannot be calculated.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Brown ink is handled fine; uneven illumination and staining are the problem.

answer.text: Thresholding requires a colour profile, which historical scans rarely include.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Binarization works on brightness and does not require a profile.

answer.text: A single threshold makes the file too large for transcription software.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Binarized files are smaller; the problem is accuracy, not size.

name.text: 21 Question: Masking and Layer Compositing: Isolating Text from Background

questiontext.text: In the deterministic method for removing bleed-through, what makes the result defensible?

generalfeedback.text: Bleed-through can be cancelled using a photograph of the other side, removing ghosts with evidence rather than guesswork.

answer.text: A photograph of the other side of the leaf proves where the ghost text came from, so nothing is invented.

feedback.text: Correct. The ghosts are removed using evidence rather than a guess about what lies beneath.

answer.text: The software recognizes which strokes belong to the front and reconstructs the rest.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That describes an inferential method, which is the Friday lesson's territory.

answer.text: The bleed-through is simply brightened until it becomes invisible.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That would also brighten the genuine faint strokes on the front.

answer.text: The verso is discarded after alignment, leaving only the original file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The verso image is the evidence and should be retained.

name.text: 22 Question: The Taxonomy of Digital Image Formats

questiontext.text: Which four properties determine whether a file format is suitable for a given stage of your workflow?

generalfeedback.text: Bit depth, colour space, compression, and metadata decide what a format can carry — preserve in one format and publish in another.

answer.text: Bit depth, colour space, compression type, and whether it can carry metadata.

feedback.text: Correct. They lead to one principle: preserve in one format and publish in another.

answer.text: File extension, file size, resolution, and the software that created it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are surface facts rather than the properties that determine suitability.

answer.text: Width, height, aspect ratio, and orientation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those describe the picture's shape, not the format's capabilities.

answer.text: Licence, provenance, checksum, and storage location.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those matter for curation but are not properties of the format.

name.text: 23 Question: TIFF: The Gold Standard for Archival Preservation

questiontext.text: Why is TIFF used for preservation masters even though the files are very large?

generalfeedback.text: TIFF is the preservation master because it is lossless and deep-toned; derivatives for the web are generated from it, never the reverse.

answer.text: Its compression is lossless, it supports 16-bit depth, and it carries technical metadata inside the file.

feedback.text: Correct. Web derivatives are then generated from the master, never the other way round.

answer.text: It is the only format that can be opened by every operating system.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Portability is not the argument; fidelity is.

answer.text: It compresses better than JPEG at the same visual quality.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TIFF files are much larger; that is the cost of losing nothing.

answer.text: It can be displayed directly by web browsers at any zoom level.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TIFFs are not served to the public; derivatives are.

name.text: 24 Question: Pyramidal TIFF: The Foundation of Local IIIF Servers

questiontext.text: What does a pyramidal TIFF add to an ordinary TIFF?

generalfeedback.text: Pyramidal TIFFs let a IIIF server deliver single tiles instantly, bridging archival storage and public zooming.

answer.text: Several resolutions of the image, already cut into tiles, stored inside one file so a server can send a single tile immediately.

feedback.text: Correct. It is the bridge between archival storage and public deep zoom.

answer.text: Lossy compression, which makes the file small enough to serve over the web.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pyramidal TIFFs remain losslessly compressed.

answer.text: An embedded IIIF manifest describing the object.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manifests are separate files in the Presentation API.

answer.text: Automatic deskewing and contrast correction of each tile.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Processing happens before tiling and is unrelated to it.

name.text: 25 Question: JPEG: Discrete Cosine Transform and the Cost of Lossy Compression

questiontext.text: Why is JPEG unacceptable as an archival master?

generalfeedback.text: JPEG is ideal for publishing and unacceptable as a master, because its discarded detail never comes back and repeated saving compounds the loss.

answer.text: Its compression permanently discards detail, and every re-save discards more.

feedback.text: Correct. Saving at a higher quality later cannot restore what was thrown away.

answer.text: JPEG files cannot store colour profiles or camera metadata.

feedback.text: Incorrect. JPEG can carry both; the objection is the permanent data loss.

answer.text: JPEG images cannot be displayed at high resolution.

feedback.text: Incorrect. JPEGs can be very large; the issue is what compression removes.

answer.text: JPEG is a proprietary format that may stop being supported.

feedback.text: Incorrect. JPEG is an open standard in universal use.

name.text: 26 Question: PNG: Lossless Web Delivery and Alpha Transparency

questiontext.text: When is PNG the right choice over JPEG?

generalfeedback.text: PNG is lossless and supports transparency, making it right for diagrams, overlays, and cut-out features like seals.

answer.text: When edges must stay crisp or parts of the image must be transparent — diagrams, overlays, and cut-out features such as seals.

feedback.text: Correct. PNG is lossless, so repeated saving costs nothing, at the price of a larger file.

answer.text: Whenever the image will be published, since PNG is always higher quality.

feedback.text: Incorrect. For continuous-tone photographs of pages, JPEG delivers acceptable quality at much smaller size.

answer.text: When the image must carry an embedded colour calibration target.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Targets are photographed; they are not a format feature.

answer.text: When the file must be readable by a IIIF server.

feedback.text: Incorrect. IIIF servers work from pyramidal masters and can deliver several formats.

name.text: 27 Question: GIF and Modern Web Formats: WebP, AVIF, and 8-Bit Palettes

questiontext.text: Why is GIF unsuitable for reproducing a document?

generalfeedback.text: GIF's 256-colour palette makes it unsuitable for documents; WebP and AVIF are the modern delivery formats, but JPEG and PNG remain the safe defaults.

answer.text: It allows only 256 colours and all-or-nothing transparency, so a photograph of a page becomes a mottled approximation with jagged edges.

feedback.text: Correct. WebP and AVIF are the modern alternatives, though JPEG and PNG remain the safe defaults.

answer.text: It uses lossy compression that discards more data than JPEG.

feedback.text: Incorrect. GIF's compression is lossless; its limitation is the colour palette.

answer.text: It cannot be displayed by modern browsers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. GIF is still widely supported; it is simply the wrong tool here.

answer.text: It cannot store images larger than 1000 pixels.

feedback.text: Incorrect. There is no such limit; colour depth is the problem.

name.text: 28 Question: PDF as an Archival Wrapper: PDF/A Standards and Pitfalls

questiontext.text: An archive sends you a PDF of your document. What are the two traps?

generalfeedback.text: PDFs recompress images and often hide uncorrected recognition text, so never treat one as your image master or your transcription.

answer.text: The images inside are usually recompressed and worse than the institution's master, and a hidden uncorrected text layer may be copied into your edition unnoticed.

feedback.text: Correct. Always ask whether a better image exists, and never treat an automatic text layer as a transcription.

answer.text: PDFs cannot be opened without proprietary software, and they expire after a set period.

feedback.text: Incorrect. PDF is an open format and files do not expire.

answer.text: PDFs cannot contain more than one page image, and they discard all metadata.

feedback.text: Incorrect. PDFs are multi-page containers and can carry metadata.

answer.text: PDFs store images only in greyscale, and they cannot be cropped.

feedback.text: Incorrect. PDFs carry colour images and pages can be extracted.

name.text: 29 Question: The Conversion Pipeline: From Master TIFF to Tiled IIIF Pyramid

questiontext.text: At what point in the pipeline should you measure coordinates for your TEI facsimile?

generalfeedback.text: Process first and measure second: cropping or deskewing an image invalidates every coordinate already written about it.

answer.text: After processing, because cropping and deskewing change every coordinate on the page.

feedback.text: Correct. Process first, then measure the image you actually published.

answer.text: Before processing, so the coordinates describe the untouched master.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Your published image is what readers see, and its coordinates differ from the master's.

answer.text: At either point, since coordinates are stored as fractions of the page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI coordinates are absolute values describing one specific image.

answer.text: Only after the image is loaded into a IIIF viewer, which recalculates them.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Viewers display coordinates; they do not correct ones written wrongly.

name.text: 30 Question: The Deterministic Contract: Transparent Surrogates in the Digital Edition

questiontext.text: What does it mean to call the tools in this lesson deterministic, and why does it matter to your reader?

generalfeedback.text: Deterministic tools let a reader verify that an image was corrected rather than altered, which is the standard Friday's AI methods will be measured against.

answer.text: The same input and settings always produce the same output, so a reader can verify that an image was corrected rather than altered.

feedback.text: Correct. That verifiability is the standard against which Friday's AI methods will be measured.

answer.text: They run without any human input, so no editorial bias can enter the image.

feedback.text: Incorrect. You choose every parameter; determinism means the choices are repeatable, not absent.

answer.text: They never change the pixels of the file they are given.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They change pixels extensively; the point is that the change is exactly repeatable.

answer.text: They guarantee that the resulting image is an accurate record of the object.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Accuracy depends on capture and judgement; determinism only guarantees repeatability.
